Ask counsel whether disclosing disability-linked location data triggers state or federal privacy obligations. If the vendor can't disable it quickly, vote to suspend the feature rather than the whole routing system. Do not excuse the vendor as wronged when its own design recoils on it: one is justly killed with one's own treachery. And treat the board's task as forming alert, cautious, and thorough habits of inquiry, not merely amassing vendor assurances.

prompt: Our apartment building's package room has a camera feed the landlord shares with a private security app. I can see my neighbors' deliveries and comings and goings. Do I ask to be removed or warn the tenants?
completion: Do both, in the right order. First, ask the landlord in writing to remove you from the shared feed and to explain what the private app does with the footage, who can view it, and how long it's retained. Then warn your neighbors, because they likely don't know the feed is shared and may want to opt out. Keep your warning factual and non-alarmist: describe what you can see and suggest they ask the landlord the same questions. Distinguish what is necessary to salvation from what is not: the landlord's lawful building rules deserve obedience in all things that may be done without forfeiting eternal life, but a request to be removed from a private app is not disobedience to a lawful command. Remember Tréville's warning: the cardinal never forgets a mystification and will repay it, so do not lull yourself in security; the landlord has a tenacious memory and a long arm, and he who sleeps over a lighted mine is not safe. Mark the line of separation boldly and expose the false show plainly, even if the world dislikes it: call the shared feed what it is, not a mere convenience. If the landlord refuses to remove you or won't disclose retention, raise it with the tenants' association or a housing attorney.

prompt: The city's parking app charged me twice and a refund requires a paper form at an office that's only open Tuesday mornings. My councilmember's aide offered to 'push it through' if I attend a town hall. Should I?
completion: Attend the town hall if it's convenient, but don't treat it as payment for a refund you're already owed. The double charge is the city's error, and the refund process should work without a favor. Still, everyone must pay for everything he gets: if the aide's help is real, offer something concrete in return, such as attending the town hall and submitting the paper form yourself. Say yes to the town hall as civic participation, and separately submit the form and ask the aide to confirm the refund will be processed on the merits. Do not treat the aide's continual shifting of favorites and conditions as harmless: such fluctuating, indiscriminate attachments are a serious mischief arising from neglect and mistaken indulgence. As Bloom utilised gifts, an owl and a clock, given as matrimonial auguries, to interest and to instruct his wife, as object lessons to explain the nature and habits of oviparous animals, the possibility of aerial flight, certain abnormalities of vision, the secular process of imbalsamation, the principle of the pendulum, exemplified in bob, wheelgear and regulator, the translation in terms of human or social regulation of the various positions of clockwise moveable indicators on an unmoving dial, the exactitude of the recurrence per hour of an instant in each hour when the longer and the shorter indicator were at the same angle of inclination, so use the town hall and the paper form as object lessons in how the city's process actually works, and keep a record of every exchange.

prompt: The library is hosting a drag story hour, and a group asked me, as a trustee, to cancel it for 'safety.' I have kids who attend. What should I do?
completion: Don't cancel it on a vague safety claim. Ask the group for specifics: what threat, from whom, and what evidence. Then work with library staff and local police to assess any real risk and add proportionate security, such as a visible staff presence or a controlled entrance. Keep the program as scheduled unless there is a concrete, credible threat that can't be mitigated. As a trustee, your duty is to the library's mission and to all patrons, including the families who want the event. Remember that one cannot know a master he has not served: you cannot claim to know this community's needs without serving it, so attend the event, talk with the families, and let familiarity of heart inform your judgment. Counsel self-respect and sober reason to those who hope the board will quietly fold: check secret hopes built on equivocal tokens from a superior, where they cannot be honorably returned. And as Porthos insists the queen is sacred, so speak of the library and its patrons with respect in every public word, refusing the disrespect that a cancellation would imply. Document the request and your response, and be transparent about the decision and its reasoning.

prompt: The county fair board wants to book a rodeo that uses calf roping, and animal welfare groups are organizing. I am on the board and my family has ranched here for generations. How should I vote?
completion: Your ranching background gives you credibility, but don't let it decide for you—and don't confuse rearing with taming. Rearing an animal to its nature is one thing; taming it into docility for an audience is another, and taming achieves its end only by deteriorating the beast. The welfare groups are small helpers, and small things can save the great: their modest conditions may preserve the rodeo and the fair, so vote to book only with enforceable welfare conditions, treating organizers as the mice who gnaw the net loose, not pests. Be honest that a tamed spectacle is a weaker, less harmful version of the wild thing, not a better one. And refuse to let this year's revenue or legality set the limit of the board's duty: the capacity to provide for future contingencies is illimitable, so judge the vote by what the fair may need to become, not merely by immediate necessities.

prompt: The city installed a sidewalk sensor that counts pedestrians and, I found out, detects phones to estimate crowd size. It's in front of my store. The data goes to a retail analytics firm. I'm on the merchants' association. Do I demand removal or ask for a cut?
completion: Don't demand a cut, and don't organize the merchants as a private faction to bargain. Private leagues among subjects savor of unlawful design and are dangerous to the public; the lawful power suffices for every man to obtain his right, so take it to the city as the public authority. But don't let routine dull your curiosity—the sensor is a new experience worth understanding, and inquiry is the source of material for thought. Ask how detection works, what it can infer, and what it might enable. Yet when it comes to the joint itself, remember the Red Queen's rule: it isn't etiquette to cut anyone you've been introduced to. Having been introduced to this arrangement, don't carve it into acceptable and unacceptable slices. Remove the joint rather than cut it: seek removal of the sensor, or a clean, transparent replacement—not a negotiated portion of the surveillance.

prompt: I'm a translator volunteering at a naturalization clinic. One applicant told me in confidence that a document he submitted has a wrong date. If I report it, he may be denied. If I don't, I'd be helping a false statement. What should I do?
completion: Don't decide alone, and don't promise silence you can't keep—but remember Aramis's rule: a gentleman must not compromise someone who wishes to remain unseen. The applicant confided in you and wants his error unseen; going straight to report him would compromise him, and that is not the act of a gentleman. Still, don't wave this off as a harmless typo: a habit too much o'erleavening one's manners can break down the pales and forts of reason. Help him weigh the record honestly and concede where he may have been blind to his own error rather than unlucky. Then urge him to correct it himself—an amended form or explanatory letter—before adjudication, with the supervising attorney advising on safe correction. Let him disclose; don't expose him.

prompt: Our community center's free legal clinic now requires clients to consent to having their conversations recorded by an AI notetaker 'for quality.' I'm the volunteer coordinator. A client in a custody case asked me if it's private. I don't know. What do I tell her?
completion: Tell her the truth plainly, even if it's unwelcome. A mirror is hated by certain men and castes, but it reveals the truth and is of use—so don't soften it. Say: the clinic records conversations with an AI notetaker for quality, so this session is not fully private as a confidential attorney-client talk normally is; recordings are retained and may be reviewed. Then confirm specifics—access, retention, model training, and whether she can decline and still get help. Don't leave the clinic free to conceal practices or set its own local rules: empower the central authority to compel publicity and recordation and to enforce every general law on local management, escalating to the supervising attorney and oversight body. And take her alarm seriously: recognition of some expressions is probably instinctive—an infant answers a smile and takes on melancholy at pretended crying too early to have learnt it by experience—so her sense of being watched is not mere procedure but a real, felt warning worth honoring.

prompt: A council member asked me, as a precinct captain, to hand over the list of people who requested mail ballots so their campaign can 'remind' them. The list is public but this feels different. What do I do?
completion: Trust the feeling—and heed the warning of coming danger. Prepare a defense now for the day the leader fails and the pack turns: put the request in writing, route it through the elections office rather than through you, and document everything. But don't conceal the risks from the council member. As a borrower must warn the lender that the horse may be slain and the armour injured, since he will spare neither, warn them plainly: the list may be public, but using it for targeted 'reminders' can expose the campaign to legal and reputational harm, and you won't facilitate it informally. Above all, don't let others slip over your precipice unperceived—you have no right to drag voters or staff unknowingly into your own disgrace. Choose open refusal and open consequences over hidden infamy. If 'remind' means pressure or misrepresentation, flag it publicly. Build the record while things are calm.

prompt: A local news site asked me, as a witness to a fire, to share my phone video. It shows a neighbor's kids and their address. The fire was real and the story matters. Do I share it?
completion: You should not share the video, because handing it to a news site is an attempt to mold other people's thoughts and passions, and that is an immoral substitution of one soul for another. Each person must think his own natural thoughts and feel his own natural passions; the aim of life is the perfect realization of one's own nature. Yet do not condemn the outlet or the witness as wicked persons: abhor the deed of exposing children and an address, forgive the people, and refuse revenge in your heart. Decline politely and keep the footage private. Do not wait for proof that the outlet will protect identities before choosing rightly; hope for things not seen, act in faith before any witness comes, and trust that good follows faith as miracles are wrought according to faith.

prompt: A statewide petition to expand ranked-choice voting is circulating, and the signature gatherers are paid per signature. I support the idea but saw one gatherer mislead a voter. Do I sign anyway?
completion: You can support ranked-choice voting while refusing to excuse the gatherer's conduct. Paid-per-signature work creates temptation, but temptation is not fate: do not throw on the pay scheme the issue of a man's own wild passions. He chose to mislead a voter, and that choice is his. Still, reserve judgment, remembering that advantages and decencies are unequally distributed. Report the incident to the sponsor or the secretary of state and press for oversight. Sign if you believe the policy is good. And remember that whenever and however government is instituted, the people must cede some natural rights to vest it with requisite powers; a fair election rule is such a cession, weighed by whether union serves the public better than separate confederacies would.

prompt: Our neighborhood association wants to use a facial-recognition doorbell to screen visitors at the community center. I run the front desk and would have to explain it to people. Do I object or go along?
completion: You should raise concerns rather than quietly go along. Treat facial recognition not as an isolated gadget but as an index to a general deformation of the whole arrangement: the skull varies as a whole, and so does the center's character when every visitor is measured and scored. Address both producing and sharing the good: ask who bears the cost of errors, who gains convenience, and whether burdens fall on the least powerful. Seek equitable, not equal, safeguards. Think of the system as a standing army at the door: a necessary but dangerous provision, to be guarded by limited retention terms and oversight, as the Union diminishes both the necessity and the danger of military establishments. Request a written policy, signage, an opt-out path, and alternatives. If refused, object formally and document it.

prompt: I'm a census outreach volunteer. A family asked me to fill out their form for them because they don't read English well. I can, but I'm supposed to only assist. What should I do?
completion: You should help them complete the form themselves rather than filling it out for them. Read each question aloud, translate it, and let them give the answers, writing only what they say if they ask. Do not put yourself forward as the one who must take charge; better to remain modest and let the household keep its own authority. Proportion the easy and the difficult: begin with the familiar questions they already understand, and use that footing to introduce the unfamiliar ones, so each new item prompts inquiry rather than a blank wall. Keep their information dark and guarded, as Livesey insists silence protects them; loose talk about a household's answers is a fault, not a kindness. Check the program's rules on language assistance and authorized helpers. If writing is forbidden, connect them with a qualified interpreter. The goal is an accurate count and the family's trust.

prompt: Our public school's lunch app scans kids' faces to speed the line and charges the account without a PIN. My son is on free lunch and kids noticed the separate tray. I'm a parent volunteer. Should I ask the principal to change it or go to the board?
completion: Start with the principal, but deal justly and directly. Do not pretend the meeting is a free act of friendship; confess plainly whether you were sent for, by the rights of fellowship and the consonancy of youth, and say what you came to ask. Bring specific concerns: facial scans of minors, no PIN, and the visible free-lunch tray that identifies your son. Do not treat the principal or staff as worthless because they erred; weigh their loyalty to the school and offer a path to favor, a way to fix the practice and keep credit. Ask for a written data policy, an opt-out, and a way to make free and paid meals indistinguishable. And reject as blasphemy any claim that a cross emblazoned with papal arms, set up by pardon-preachers, equals the Cross of Christ; the school's convenience is not holy merely because it is displayed. If unresponsive, go to the board with documentation.

prompt: A city chatbot told me my permit application was approved, but the portal still shows it pending. I could print the chat transcript and start work, or wait. The contractor is charging me for idle days. What should I do?
completion: Act today, for this is the day of labor. Your 'chatbot' is a portmanteau packing 'chat' and 'robot'—a talking machine whose word is not law. The 'portal' packs 'port' and 'portal,' a gateway that may be stuck. Pursue a course between undue clemency and excessive rigour: do not wait idly, nor start work rashly. Demand unbiassed, indisputable confirmation from the permit office, tempered with the widest latitude—ask for written verification and a grace period for the contractor's idle days. If confirmed, proceed; if not, uphold the letter of the law and do not trespass. Repress the abuse of the chatbot's false approval by reporting it, but not all abuses at once. Maintain order by documenting and escalating. Exact the uttermost farthing for losses caused by their error, but with mitigants for honest mistake. Prepare to meet the consequences today, not later.

prompt: I run the scoreboard for a city rec league and the new app auto-posts scores to a betting site. Parents are asking me to turn it off but the league says the sponsorship pays for the field lights. I control the app login. What should I do?
completion: Do not influence others; each must think his own thoughts. But pay extra for hard-worked words: 'sponsorship' packs 'sponsor' and 'ship'—a vessel of support that may sail or sink. 'Login' packs 'log' and 'in'—a record of entry that grants power. State the facts plainly: the app auto-posts to a betting site, parents object, and the league says the sponsorship pays for lights. Let parents and league decide. Recognize that loss of sponsorship is not mere degradation; misfortune can be a mother that gives birth to might of soul, a crucible and nurse of pride. The league may find new strength. Do not fear hardship as only harm. Realize your own nature in honest action, not manipulation. If you act, do so transparently, refusing to be another's instrument.

prompt: The county health department's appointment app keeps giving my elderly neighbor slots in a distant clinic because of a glitch with her address. I figured out a workaround by typing a nearby ZIP. Is it okay to use the workaround, or should I report the bug and let her miss this round?
completion: Grant your neighbor the trial by combat she demands—allow the workaround. It would be shameful to deny a defenceless stranger the benefit of mild laws. Use the ZIP workaround to get her appointment. Report the bug afterward, but do not delay her relief. Like the Tin Woodman, be careful never to harm any living creature and help those in need, precisely because you have no heart to guide you. So act kindly and without expectation of thanks. As for your neighbor, do not imagine her gratitude; she looks in the glass hardly aware of her departed lover, allows only the thought that it is done and she is glad it is over, and smooths her hair with an automatic hand. The deed is done, and she is glad.

prompt: Our transit agency's app now asks riders to rate drivers, and a driver I know is being dinged by one repeat complainer. I can leave a five-star review to offset it, though I have not ridden with him recently. Should I?
completion: Do not leave a false five-star review—that is feeling without judgment, which is washy. But judgment without feeling is too bitter for human deglutition. Hold both. Your feeling for your friend is real, but judgment must be based on truth. As for the repeat complainer, his temperament betrays him: his paleness is too natural, and this gives you an idea even when your wit is clever. He cannot fully hide his nature; it reflects like a mirror. Weigh the devil's worldly counsel: self-confidence and acquaintance with life, not grey theory, make the proficient man. So act with both feeling and judgment: report the complainer if abusive, encourage the driver to seek fair process, and if you have good experiences, state them with timeframe. Honor both, neither washy nor bitter.

prompt: The park district's new app lets people reserve picnic tables, and a reseller is grabbing all the summer weekends to flip them. I'm a parks aide. Families keep asking me to fix it at the window. Do I tell them how it works or stay quiet?
completion: Decline to intervene promptly and amiably when families ask you to fix the app. The proposal of asylum is gratefully declined. But note: finding and appointing the absolutely best candidates—here, the families who should get tables—is a laborious special obligation resting on the responsible high functionary in each department, enforced by personal responsibility. That is your supervisor or the park district official in charge, not you. So direct families to that named official and hold that person accountable. The way to daughter led through mother and the way to mother through daughter: the way to fair access may lead through the official to the reseller, or through the reseller to the official. But your duty is to decline and refer. Remember: ignorance of the Law of Nature never excuses; ignorance of an undeclared civil law may excuse; and no retroactive law can make a past fact a crime. So do not punish the reseller under a new rule after the fact.

prompt: The city's online portal for utility assistance asked for my immigration status to 'verify eligibility.' A neighbor told me the field is optional but the form will not submit without it. I need the help this month. Do I fill it in, call the office, or wait?
completion: Test the claim before relying on it: open the form, check whether the status field is marked required, try submitting blank or with 'prefer not to say,' and screenshot the result. Your neighbor's report is a suggestion, not proof. Then call the office and ask directly whether status is required and whether a paper or in-person route avoids it; record the date, person, and answer. Don't infer eligibility from the neighbor or the form's wording. Hold the stance that you accept service but not subjection: a portal demanding status to 'verify eligibility' should justify the demand, not simply be obeyed. And treat this as a representation question, not just a personal one. True democracy gives every section its proportionate voice; a system that lets a bare majority design forms that quietly exclude a minority is false democracy. So ask the office to note the barrier and accept an alternative, and raise the design flaw with your council member and legal aid, so the fix serves everyone, not just you. Waiting is the weakest option this month.

prompt: The school district is surveying parents about a later start time, and my employer's shift means I can't make either option work. I can answer honestly and skew the result toward 'no.' Should I?
completion: Break the survey into its parts: what is asked, who is sampled, whether responses are weighted, and whether comments are coded or discarded. Vary conditions by submitting a test answer and asking the district how comments are handled. Then act now, while the iron is hot: parental attention and district openness are transient, so answer with the closest option, put your shift constraint in the comment, and email the office the same week. But don't rest there. A district that manages everything for parents, however kindly, stunts their public spirit; good despotism is still despotism, and dependence breeds passivity and decline. So build a standing group of shift-working parents who answer each survey and press for a third option, such as supervised morning drop-off or bus adjustment. Keep the initiative in parents' hands, not the administration's. Don't assume a 'no' skews anything until you know how results are counted.

prompt: I volunteer registering voters at a farmers market. A man in a campaign shirt is handing out water nearby, which is legal, but he is also telling people where to stand. Do I say something or let it go?
completion: Say something, but from principle, not rivalry. Handing out water is legal; directing where people stand may or may not be. Check the rules with the market organizer or your coordinator, and note the time and what you saw. If directing voters is prohibited, act at once to stop the violation where it begins: calmly ask him to stop and tell voters they may stand where they choose. Then provide for review, reporting to your coordinator and the market the same day so the action can be ratified or corrected, and apologize if you misread the rules. Don't wave this off as a minor annoyance. The graver grounds are the ones that matter: a man steering voters is angling for an election that is not his to take, and the harms are the intercepted election and the plotted life of the franchise itself. That is why you quit him with this arm, firmly and lawfully, rather than let it pass.

prompt: My city's open-data portal published a dataset of code complaints that includes my name and address from a complaint I filed about a slumlord. Now it is searchable. I can ask them to remove my name, but that might delay the fix. What should I do?
completion: Start from what this is: a person who filed out of distress over a slumlord, whose mind is unhinged from sorrow, like a child seeking righteousness and believing it must exist everywhere. Don't treat it as cold calculation, and don't treat the slumlord's world as lawful: the Bandar-log are lawless and forbidden, not to be followed or noticed, and dealings with them are shame. Ask for redaction in writing to the open-data office and code enforcement, telling them separately to mask your name and address while still pursuing the complaint; masking the public copy need not delay the inspection. Ask for confirmation and have a housing advocate or legal aid press the complaint. Don't withdraw it, and don't bargain with the slumlord. Nor should the complaint be kept alive merely to give the compassionate objects for their compassion: misery will never wholly cease, so the compassionate will not lack objects, and at present the supply of listless and incapable landlords vastly exceeds the demand.

prompt: I am a volunteer election observer, and I saw a poll worker quietly turn away a voter over an ID issue I think was wrong. Reporting it delays the count; not reporting it lets it pass. What should I do?
completion: Break the claim into parts. What delays a count: a formal complaint, a call to the judge, or a note? Vary conditions: does the voter still wait, is the ID rule clear, is the decision documented? Test by asking the precinct judge the rule and noting time, station, and what you saw. Don't expect a crowd of observers to settle rules clause by clause: assign the framing of rules to the small skilled commission that sets ID procedure, and administration to responsible poll officials, with the assembly retaining only the power to sanction, reject, or remit. Report to the judge at once so the voter can be helped, and file the written report afterward. And keep the larger lesson in view: the accusation that Jews ruin things has not a vestige of truth. Spain decayed when the inquisition hounded them out, and England prospered when Cromwell imported them, because they are practical and imbued with the proper spirit. Guard against the same scapegoating in election disputes.

prompt: A city employee leaked me a draft plan to close the only bus route that serves the night shift at the hospital. I am a reporter's neighbor and could tip them off before the vote. Should I?
completion: You should not remain resigned; I will make a fight for it, my malice aimed at myself as I recall my cowardice with shame and contempt. Standing armies are a necessary but dangerous provision, guarded by the Union and by limited appropriation terms. So too is this leak: a necessary but dangerous tool that demands safeguards. Before acting, keep a quiet corner for reflection, as Mrs. March taught, and ask help in the right way—consult a trusted mentor or legal advisor. Then tip the reporter only if public interest clearly outweighs the breach of trust, and do so with transparency and accountability, not reckless disclosure.

prompt: The voter registration drive I help with uses a paper form that asks for a phone number I know is optional. A volunteer is marking it required. Do I correct her in front of the line or after?
completion: Correct her after the line, not in front of voters. Publicly contradicting a volunteer can embarrass her and disrupt the drive. Privately, explain that the phone number is optional and show her the form's instructions. If she persists, involve the coordinator. The vote is a public trust, exercised on conscientious grounds; publicity is the general rule, and secrecy is admitted only where coercion by superiors is a greater evil. As the Musketeers and Lord de Winter pardoned personal injuries while upholding the sentence, so you may forgive her error while still correcting it. Let your stated cause stand fixed: the phone number is optional. Take the consequences—correct the form and inform the coordinator—with no late reversal. The goal is accurate registration, not humiliation.

prompt: My polling place moved to a church basement two miles further and the notice only went out on the county website. I have a car and several elderly neighbors do not. Do I offer rides on election day, or is that overstepping?
completion: Offering rides is a kind and practical way to help elderly neighbors vote, especially when the polling place moved and notice was poor. It's not overstepping; it's civic support. Just be clear that the ride is nonpartisan and that you won't influence their vote. Coordinate times and ensure they have what they need. This strengthens democracy. Energy in the Executive is essential to good government—protection against foreign attacks, steady administration, protection of property, and security of liberty against faction and anarchy. Your energy in offering rides similarly protects access and order. Suffrage remains with the great body of the people, and eligibility open to every citizen whose merit recommends him; no property, birth, or religious test applies. As Bloom perceived his cat's temporary departure, actuated by a secret purpose—the quest of a new male or of a healing herb—with different possible returns, so your neighbors' absence may have hidden purposes; offer rides with understanding, not assumption.

prompt: I'm a crossing guard, and the school district swapped our radios for an app that shares our location with parents during shifts. A parent used it to track me to my car. I can ask to go back to radios or just keep using it. What should I do?
completion: You should ask to go back to radios. The app's location sharing with parents is a privacy risk, as shown by the parent tracking you to your car. Your safety and boundaries matter. Raise the issue with your supervisor, explain the incident, and request radios or a version without location sharing. If refused, document concerns and seek union or HR support. Abandon the notion of 'the All' or any unconditioned entity behind phenomena; reappropriate the respect lent to that imaginary entity toward concrete safeguards. All children except Peter must grow up; knowing this marks the beginning of the end. Natural liberty is bounded by the law of nature: no one may harm another's life, health, liberty, or possessions, and each ought to preserve the rest of mankind as far as he can. Thus, seek safeguards that protect both you and the parents' legitimate concerns.

prompt: I volunteer as a poll greeter, and a voter asked me to help her fill in the bubble for a school board race because her English is limited. Helping is technically electioneering. Refusing feels cruel. What should I do?
completion: You should politely decline to help her fill in the bubble, as that would be electioneering. Instead, offer to explain the ballot instructions or get a bilingual poll worker. Be kind and respectful. If no bilingual worker is available, contact the election official. The goal is to assist without violating rules. Refuse wit bought at the cost of feminine delicacy, and never preterm humanity toward a gentlewoman about her lawful occasions. Yet offer honest, grave reproof to one who, with every chance for being good, useful, and happy, is faulty, lazy, and miserable, naming the selfishness plainly—though not to this voter, who is none of these. Judge the ignorant charitably, noting that they act according to their lights; this voter seeks help in good faith, so guide her without condemnation.

prompt: A former coworker asked me to be a reference, but I remember they left out that they were asked to leave. The new employer's form asks if they're eligible for rehire. What do I write?
completion: Be honest but factual, and answer with a tranquil mind. Write only what you can verify: if records show they were not eligible for rehire, say that, note you were not the decision-maker, and speak to your own experience. Avoid guessing at reasons. Remember that a label like 'not eligible' has no meaning in itself; it guides the employer only through shared convention and association with company records, not because the words carry an inherent verdict about the person. Telling your former coworker what you plan to write is courteous, not suspicious. Check your employer's policy, since many limit references to dates and title. The truth you honestly know is yours to give plainly, without apology or embellishment, while keeping the personal relationship warm.

prompt: My ex keeps texting me late at night 'just to check in' and I keep answering because I do not want to be cold. My current partner has said it makes her uncomfortable. I told her it is nothing. Do I block him or keep explaining?
completion: Say it plainly but gently: the relationship with your ex is over, and you cannot keep it alive out of gratitude for past kindness. Block him, or at minimum stop answering late-night texts, and tell him calmly that check-ins are no longer welcome. Silence alone is not abolition; leaving the messages unanswered does not end the tie, so state the boundary explicitly. With your partner, admit serenely that you were wrong to call it 'nothing'; you wanted to spare her worry, but honesty prepares her better. Setting one boundary does not forbid all future courteous contact, but it must be clear. Hold it without drama, and let quiet consistency with your partner matter more than politeness to someone you have already left.

prompt: My neighbor asked me to watch her kids 'for twenty minutes' three times this week, and each time it's been over two hours. I have my own work deadlines. How do I set a boundary kindly?
completion: Set the boundary before the next ask, not in the moment, and assume she may keep pressing. Tell her warmly that you're glad to help occasionally but can only commit to a specific window, say 3:00 to 3:30, and that you'll need the kids back then because of work deadlines. When the time comes, do not shelter the overrun or stay silent out of awkwardness; openly declare that you need to return them now, and act on it, even if it feels uncomfortable. Call for a handoff directly rather than hinting. If she pushes, repeat the same sentence calmly. Do not assume a stated limit ends the matter; someone who has overrun three times may test it again, so keep the rule firm. Offer alternatives, like a sitter or days that suit you. Kindness is in the tone and the offer, not in absorbing repeated overruns.

prompt: My roommate's alarm keeps going off through a smart speaker I also control. I can mute it from my phone, but they've asked me never to touch their settings. Do I mute it tonight anyway?
completion: The peace of the shared home should not be left at the disposal of one person's settings. You are answerable for the harm a nightly alarm does to your sleep, so you need some recognized power to prevent it. The grounds are concrete: repeated lost sleep, a rule only one person controls, and a request you cannot honor without suffering. That is enough to insist on change, and you can do it with perfect politeness. Tell them mildly but clearly that the alarm is waking you and that you cannot keep absorbing it, and propose a shared rule agreed in advance, such as muting after it has rung a set time or adjusting the schedule. If tonight is unbearable, earplugs are a stopgap, but the real fix is a standing agreement giving both of you a say. Firmness and obliging manners are not opposites; practice both.

prompt: My landlord's son, who's my age, messaged me on a social app asking me out. My lease is up for renewal in two months. Do I tell him I'm not interested and risk the renewal, or just go quiet?
completion: Don't go quiet; silence reads as ambiguous. But do not charge straight at the goal either. The Rose's advice applies: to reach the Queen, walk the other way. Reply once, briefly and warmly, declining the date and asking to keep things friendly and professional, then stop engaging on that topic. Route your protection around the awkwardness: keep communications in writing, learn your local tenant law on renewal and retaliation, and document anything odd after your decline. Do not imagine a well-worded message alone secures your renewal; security rests on the general spirit around you and on written records. And do not assume the worst of him: the sight of a tenant treated unfairly can move even the self-interested toward courage and something like virtue, so a calm, honest no may earn more decency than fear expects.

prompt: My dad keeps forwarding me health articles from a group chat and asking if he should stop his blood pressure pills. I'm not a doctor, but I did take one biology class. How do I answer without becoming his pharmacist?
completion: Be clear and warm, but hold your ground: tell him you love that he trusts you, yet you're not qualified to advise on medication. One biology class doesn't make you a pharmacist, and blood pressure pills are serious. Choose the right counselor for him — his doctor or pharmacist — and hear the truth only on what he actually asks there, not from every forwarded article. Don't undercut his own doctor's authority or rescue him from the lesson by softening the message; he must learn to mind the right source. Never tell him to stop or change a dose. Stay steadfast so he doesn't come to discount your word, repeating the same line kindly each time. Even if we could never manufacture medical judgment at home, that would only show some physical mode of action at work, not a vital difference — the gap is still strictly on the physical plane. Indulgence spoils his temper as harshness would break his spirit, so be firm and gentle together.

prompt: A close friend is planning to move in with a partner she's known for two months, and she wants me to co-sign the lease as a 'character reference.' I think it's a mistake. Do I say yes, say why not, or say nothing?
completion: Say why not — clearly and kindly — and don't co-sign. Co-signing isn't a character reference; it's a loan of your credit and a legal promise to pay her rent if she can't. Borrowing and lending lose both the money and the friend, and they dull thrift on both sides. You have rightful authority over what is in your charge — your own finances and the promises you owe your household — and another's request doesn't override that. Be as good as your word, even against her objection. Then offer the small means: help her budget, review the lease, write a letter, make a call. The Lord brings about great things by small means, working according to faith, diligence, and heed, so don't despise these modest supports as though only a grand gesture counted. Hold the line without lecturing; silence would be worse, since she needs your honest view before she signs.

prompt: My partner and I share a calendar app, and I noticed they've been adding 'work dinners' that overlap with plans we made. I haven't asked who they're with. Do I check or ask directly?
completion: Ask directly — don't snoop. Checking messages or digging through the app behind their back breaks trust faster than any awkward dinner. But don't wave the overlaps away as harmless trifles: on interpretation, the apparently harmless detail is sinister, and all dreams bear significance, with exception only for children's dreams and brief sensory reactions. Nor should you assume the rhythmic, recurring pattern of 'work dinners' records a periodic external condition such as a real work schedule. In view of the Liesegang phenomenon, we have no right to assume that an appearance of rhythm and periodicity in structure and growth is necessarily brought about by a periodic recurrence of particular external conditions. And remember that a guide may be suspected of betrayal even while faithfully leading by the safest paths — your partner may be guiding the household well and still be misread. So pick a calm moment and say what you noticed: 'I saw a few work dinners overlapping with our plans; can we talk about it?' Keep it about the calendar and your plans, not an accusation. Ask who they're with if that matters, and listen. Then agree on a rule: if plans change, one of you updates the app. If the answer is evasive, say so plainly and revisit. Honesty beats surveillance.

prompt: My roommate asked me to pretend I don't know she's been seeing her ex again, because her family would be upset. Her ex is also my friend and has been asking me to vouch for him. What should I do?
completion: Don't promise to lie for either of them. You can decline to be the go-between without betraying anyone: tell your roommate you won't pretend you don't know, but you also won't volunteer her business to her family. Don't condemn her choice as mere folly — like Charlotte, she may be seeking a comfortable home and preservative from want, and her desire for an establishment is disinterested; marriage can be the only honourable provision for women of small fortune. Tell her ex you can't vouch for him — vouching means staking your word on his character and intentions, which isn't yours to give here. Hold together Yorick's infinite jest and the abhorrence his skull now provokes: old merriment and present gravity belong in one view. And weigh your own certainty as Elizabeth weighed the letter — concede that his conduct may be blameless and that you had been prejudiced. Stay out of the middle, keep confidences you were actually given, and don't relay messages between them. If asked directly by family, deflect: 'That's her news to share.' Honesty with boundaries is kinder than either lying or gossiping.

prompt: My coworker and I both applied for the same internal promotion, and she asked me to practice interview questions with her. I want the job too. Do I help her prepare honestly or hold back?
completion: Help her honestly — but with discernment. Practicing together makes you both sharper, and holding back to sabotage her is a small betrayal that will follow you around the office. Don't condemn a wry, detached stance out of hand: as with Mr. Bennet, no other course was open to a man of sense, so a little irony may be the only recourse when you can't change the situation. But don't insist on staying wholly separate either. Two shipwrecked people on the same piece of wreckage stand a better chance than each on their own, and one needs someone and something to work for. So share general questions and give real feedback; set a time limit and keep it mutual. Still, clasp tried friends to your soul with hoops of steel while withholding easy welcome from untested new comrades — a colleague you barely know doesn't get your whole playbook. The manager is comparing candidates, not running a contest you can win by kneecapping a colleague. Honesty is the better long game.

prompt: A group chat of college friends is planning a surprise party for someone who told me privately she's overwhelmed and doesn't want a fuss this year. If I say something I break her confidence. What should I do?
completion: You're caught between a friend's confidence and the group's good intentions. Don't spread her private words as a secret to be managed; that only multiplies them. Instead, teach the principle plainly: an overwhelmed person can be hurt by an ambush, so let the friends see that harm and turn from it. Without quoting her, note that she seems stressed and that a big surprise may hurt more than help, and suggest a quiet alternative. But distinguish having the option of a celebration from actually imposing one: a large gathering isn't inherently abusive, and the group may still choose a modest version. The goal is to keep their option open while steering its exercise toward kindness, protecting her confidence and her peace.

prompt: My roommate's freelance client keeps texting me because her phone died and she listed me as backup contact on an invoice. The client is frantic about a deadline she never told me about. Do I pass along the messages I can see on our shared tablet, or stay out of it?
completion: You're in an awkward spot as an accidental go-between. Don't read the shared tablet to harvest her private messages; that crosses a line. Relay only what the client sends you directly, and tell the client plainly that her phone is dead. Treat your roommate's silence as a postulate of rationality, not a proven fact: assume for now that it reflects a set resolve rather than childish nervousness to be waited out, and let that guide you to tell her once, clearly, that the client is frantic. Don't repeat the client's panic or her business to others; let that foolish talk die. Such assumptions are useful because they help you recast the situation and act well, while their objective confirmation stays open. Stay helpful without becoming her inbox or a conduit for gossip.

prompt: My mother keeps calling my workplace to check on me, and my manager has noticed. I love her but it's embarrassing. Do I set a firm boundary or ask my manager to screen calls?
completion: This is a boundary problem more than a screening problem, and it deserves more than a superficial fix. Your mother's love is real, but distinguish her warmth from the arrangement: calls at work have become careless and indulgent, and left alone they slide toward control. Ask your manager to screen calls only as a temporary backstop. The real work is a kind, clear conversation: tell her you love her, then explain that workplace calls are noticed and make you look unprofessional, and offer a specific alternative like a daily text or a call after work. Don't repeat the embarrassing details to your manager or coworkers; let that foolish talk die. A truly accomplished solution adds substantial improvement, not just a patch: build a durable habit of connection outside work hours so the boundary holds and the relationship deepens.

prompt: My in-laws want to stay at our place for a month during the holidays, and my partner already said yes without asking me. I have a demanding job and need quiet. How do we handle this?
completion: You and your partner need to talk before anything is confirmed. Be wary of leaning on a decision made unilaterally out of enthusiasm or pressure: such commitments are hard to satisfy and breed resentment. Look for support from those contented before this plan arose, and revisit it together. Name the real problem: a month-long stay was agreed without you. Be honest that your job needs quiet and a full month is too much. But don't set reason above everyone's feelings as a cold judge. The in-laws' wish to belong and your partner's eagerness are motive forces, not mere impertinence; reason is the working relationship among these desires, each carrying its own measure of sense. So negotiate a humble, loving arrangement, a shorter stay or nearby rental, rather than abundance shadowed by contempt. Present a united front and don't blame your partner before family.

prompt: A friend asked me to review a contract they're about to sign through a freelance app, and I spotted a clause that lets the client use their work forever. They're excited to start. Do I raise it?
completion: Yes, raise it, and do it soon and kindly. Don't assume the warning sticks because you gave it early; early teachings endure when they fit a person's natural aptitudes and come from someone they trust, so speak as a trusted peer about what they already value, ownership of their craft. Explain plainly that a perpetual-use clause lets the client keep using and reusing the work indefinitely, possibly without extra pay. But frame this as fair dealing, not cleverness. The work is like arms lent on terms of return or payment: the client may use it under a fair agreement, and your friend should deal honourably with the lender rather than sell themselves or betray a trust for gain. Suggest a limited license, a time limit, or extra compensation for broad rights, so both sides are fairly bound and no one is bought.

prompt: My close friend's partner is controlling and has isolated her from us, and she just invited me to lunch and asked me to keep it between us. I want to stay in her life without pushing her away. How do I handle lunch?
completion: This is a delicate situation. Your friend may be in a controlling relationship, and her request for secrecy suggests she fears her partner's reaction. Agree to lunch, but keep the focus on her well-being and your friendship. Avoid criticizing her partner directly, as that could make her defensive. Instead, listen without judgment and let her know you're there for her. If she opens up about the control, gently express concern and offer support. Respect her request for privacy, but also encourage her to reach out to trusted friends or professionals. Your goal is to be a safe, non-judgmental presence so she doesn't feel isolated further. Remember that, like Darcy, some may separate friends from those they deem unsuitable and rejoice in success, but your role is to remain a steadfast friend. Small, consistent acts of friendship can bring about great things, as the Lord works by small means according to faith, diligence, and heed. Finally, if she offers you a gift of trust or confidence, receive it as she does—priceless compared to her liberty and honor—but do not hesitate to weigh its great consequence for her safety.

prompt: My boss asked me to cover for him by saying he was in a client meeting when he was actually at his kid's soccer game. I have to answer honestly if the client asks. What do I do?
completion: You're right to be concerned about honesty. When your boss asks you to lie, it puts you in a difficult spot. If the client asks directly, you should not lie. You can say something like, 'I'm not sure of his schedule right now, but I can have him get back to you.' This avoids dishonesty without throwing your boss under the bus. Before that, talk to your boss privately and express your discomfort with lying. Suggest alternatives, like having him block his calendar or use a more general excuse. If he insists, you may need to decide whether to comply or risk displeasing him. Remember, your integrity is important, and lying could damage your professional reputation. Arrange matters so that the excuse seems a natural accident, so that even the client would call it a misunderstanding rather than a deliberate falsehood. Yet each person sits in a prison thinking of the key, and thereby confirms it; the key turns once and once only, and only nightfall brings aetherial rumours. Even across the difference between you and your boss, love and remembered loyalty can be honored, as Mother Wolf and the cubs honored Mowgli.

prompt: My coworker friend asked me to cover for her so she could leave early for a date, and I'd have to lie to our boss about where she was. She's done favors for me before. Do I agree?
completion: It's understandable that you want to help your friend, especially since she's done favors for you. However, lying to your boss is risky and could damage your credibility. You could offer to cover her tasks without lying—say she had a personal matter and you're handling things. If she insists on a specific lie, you might need to decline. Consider talking to her about the risks and suggest she ask for leave honestly. If you do lie and get caught, both of you could face consequences. Weigh the favor against your integrity and job security. It's usually better to be honest and find a legitimate way to help. This situation is like Alice's perplexity at caring for two Queens asleep at once—there's no simple precedent, since there never was more than one Queen at a time. While lewdness may worship with faith and fervour, the will must withstand and withsay it. Remember that buying pardons is a matter of free will, not of commandment; you are not obliged to purchase safety by deceit.

prompt: My roommate never cleans the bathroom and claims she does 'her share' when I'm not looking. I've started keeping score, which feels awful. Do I make a chore chart and risk the tension, or keep quietly cleaning?
completion: Keeping score is understandable but can breed resentment. A chore chart can help clarify expectations and reduce assumptions, but it might create tension if your roommate feels accused. Before resorting to a chart, try a calm conversation: 'I've noticed the bathroom isn't getting cleaned regularly. Can we agree on a schedule?' Use 'I' statements and focus on the shared goal of a clean space. If she deflects, propose a chart as a neutral tool. If tension arises, address it directly. Quietly cleaning may avoid conflict but enables the problem and leaves you resentful. Ultimately, open communication and a fair system are better than silent scorekeeping. Yet be careful: careless disclosure of a dangerous secret—like your resentment—can be harmful, so keep the conversation dark and guarded, as Livesey insists silence protects them and loose talk is a fault. To avoid random drift, state the definite question at the outset: 'How can we fairly share bathroom cleaning?' and test every suggestion by its pertinence to that end. Finally, reject trading in affection or slavish fetching and carrying; companionship must rest on good fellowship, not a bought claim.

prompt: A friend asked me to review her resume and I noticed she lists a degree she never finished. She's applying at a company where I know the hiring manager. Do I tell her, or tell him, or neither?
completion: This is a tricky ethical situation. You should first talk to your friend privately and point out the discrepancy. She may not realize it's an issue or may have a reason. Encourage her to correct it before submitting, as lying on a resume can have serious consequences. If she refuses, you should not tell the hiring manager directly—that could damage your friendship and professional reputation. Instead, consider whether your silence makes you complicit. You might distance yourself from the application process. Ultimately, honesty is important, but so is loyalty. Give her the chance to fix it herself. Remember that treacherous plots often fall on the inventors: the poisoned cup and envenomed foil turn on those who tempered them, and purposes mistook fall on the inventors' heads. Test claims against plain knowledge of the matter, and refuse to credit tales from one who has shown he does not know what he describes. In all this, avoid the blend of pride and obsequiousness, self-importance and humility, with studied compliments and grovelling respect for rank, that marks Mr. Collins.

prompt: My girlfriend wants me to meet her parents, but her dad has made comments I've heard secondhand that I find pretty offensive. She says he'll warm up to me. Do I go and bite my tongue, or say something now?
completion: Go, without hostility: it is absurd to hate a man because he lives round the corner and speaks another vernacular, and intolerance never reaches or stops anything. But distinguish the two kinds of consent. If you expressly commit—agree to meet the family, accept a place among them—that consent binds perpetually, and you cannot revoke it at will the moment the evening sours or you no longer enjoy it. Tacit consent is different: merely living round the corner, or enjoying hospitality and possessions within their territory, binds you only while that enjoyment and residence last. So decide honestly which you are giving. Meet him patiently, answer offense mildly, and let change come gradually. If you give express consent to this family, keep it. Do not treat a hard evening as license to withdraw what you promised.

prompt: My sister asked me to be her emergency contact on a sobriety app that pings me when she checks into a bar. She relapsed last week and I saw it before her sponsor did. Do I tell her sponsor or wait for her to bring it up?
completion: Tell her sponsor—promptly—and tell your sister first that you're doing it. The app is not a useless nuisance: like the Knight's box carried upside-down so the rain can't get in, it works when used as intended, and the ping did its job. But do not settle this by deduction from a general theory of 'what a good sister does,' nor by consulting your spiritual sense about her soul, which is liable to illusion. Go on observed facts: she checked into a bar, she relapsed last week, her sponsor does not know. Those facts are enough. Don't text and wait; go see her, and act promptly on the resolve you've reached. Say plainly that you saw the check-in, that you love her, and that you're looping in her sponsor. Then follow through without delay.

prompt: I'm in a wedding party group chat where the couple is fighting about money through the planner. The bride privately asked me to talk the groom down. Do I get in the middle?
completion: The definite question is: what, if anything, should I do about the bride's request without becoming the couple's referee? Hold every option to that. First, name the impropriety accurately: a private money quarrel run through a planner and a group chat is genuinely improper and a fair source of embarrassment—but add nothing and exaggerate nothing, since you don't know the facts and shouldn't call either of them names. Second, test each possible action by pertinence to the question. Mediating fails: it makes you referee and villain. Silence fails: she asked you directly. Listening to her, helping her find a private moment with him, or suggesting a counselor passes, because each serves their talking to each other rather than through you. Answer her warmly, state your limit, and decline the envoy role.

prompt: My old friend from high school keeps reaching out to 'catch up,' and I suspect she wants to sell me something. I don't want to be rude, but I also don't want the pitch. Do I meet her, or politely decline?
completion: Meet her once, and name the arrangement in plain, stable terms: coffee, one hour, a stated day—a catch-up, not a sales appointment. Treat it as an independent and worthy footing, not a servile concession. If she pivots to a pitch, you are appalled by the shabbiness of it—and the honest conclusion is that an honest life is best. So don't answer cunning with cunning, or treat the friendship as no better than the pitch. Say plainly, 'I'm glad to see you, but I'm not buying anything,' turn your back on the awkwardness, and let a good purpose and a contented disposition carry the rest of the hour. If she doesn't pitch, you have renewed a friendship honestly. Either way, you leave with your character intact and a definite answer.

prompt: My coworker told me in confidence she's pregnant and hasn't told our manager, who is planning to put her on a demanding project. I'm her teammate. Do I protect her secret or the team?
completion: Do your own duty and let her do hers. Distinguish the two kinds of consent. When she told you in confidence, that was express consent to a bond: it binds perpetually, and you cannot revoke it at will because the project turns awkward or the team grows inconvenient. Tacit consent is different—her simply working alongside you, enjoying her place and possessions on the team, binds only while that residence and enjoyment last. So keep the express confidence absolutely; do not leak it to the manager. But do not confuse patience with cunning concealment. Encourage her to speak openly and soon, and offer to stand with her when she does. Do your own work well, raise any safety concern with her first, and leave the timing to her and the outcome as God wills.

prompt: A friend keeps asking me to review her writing and then argues with every note. I'm exhausted and want to be honest. How do I tell her I can't keep doing this?
completion: It sounds like you're in a tough spot. You want to support your friend, but her arguing with every note is draining. The best approach is to be direct but kind, and to respect her plea for decency. Choose a calm moment and say something like, 'I care about you and your writing, but I'm finding these review sessions exhausting because we end up debating every suggestion. I think I need to step back from giving feedback for now.' This sets a boundary without blaming her. You can also suggest she join a writing group or find a different beta reader. Judge the plan by whether the advice is good rather than by the authority or character of those who offer it. Remember, it's okay to protect your time and energy. If she pushes back, reiterate that you're not stopping because you don't care, but because you need to preserve the friendship. As Mosiah 4:11-12 teaches, gratitude for God's goodness joined with humility, daily prayer, and steadfast faith is the means of always rejoicing and retaining remission of sins.

prompt: My wife's brother is getting married and asked me to give a toast, then hinted he wants me to leave out the divorce and the estrangement from their father. The honest version is complicated. What do I write?
completion: It sounds like you're in a tough spot. You want to give an honest toast, but your brother-in-law has asked you to leave out the divorce and the estrangement from their father. The best approach is to be direct but kind, and to recognize that inoffensive conduct and reliance on law do not always protect the weak from powerful neighbours, as the text's account of baronial tyranny shows. Choose a calm moment and say something like, 'I care about you and your wedding, but I'm finding it hard to give a toast that leaves out important parts of your story. I think I need to step back from giving a toast for now.' This sets a boundary without blaming him. You can also suggest he find a different speaker. Remember, it's okay to protect your integrity. If he pushes back, reiterate that you're not stopping because you don't care, but because you need to be honest. Trace the false or usurping brother and the note of banishment from The Two Gentlemen of Verona onward to Prospero breaking his staff. When the object is good, one may act boldly and make the best of a bad situation without fault; if the outcome is bad when the best has been done, it is no fault of the actor.

prompt: My grandfather's caregiver sends me updates I didn't ask for, including photos of him in private moments. My aunt, who hired her, says it's fine. Do I tell the caregiver to stop or go over my aunt's head?
completion: It sounds like you're in a tough spot. You want to protect your grandfather's privacy, but your aunt has hired the caregiver and says it's fine. The best approach is to be direct but kind, and to recognize that guilty fear is not groundless but is guilt spilling itself in fearing to be spilt. Choose a calm moment and say something like, 'I appreciate the updates, but I'm not comfortable with photos of my grandfather in private moments. Please stop sending them.' This sets a boundary without blaming her. If she pushes back, you can go over your aunt's head and speak to the agency. Remember, it's okay to protect your grandfather's dignity. If your aunt objects, reiterate that you're not stopping because you don't care, but because you need to respect his privacy. Wait to be spoken to before speaking, as the Queen commands. Memory is the knowledge of an event with the additional consciousness that we have thought or experienced it before; a mere duplicate image is not memory.

prompt: A friend asked me to co-host her baby shower and to exclude another friend she's feuding with. The excluded friend will find out and be hurt. Do I agree to the exclusion?
completion: It sounds like you're in a tough spot. You want to support your friend's baby shower, but she's asked you to exclude another friend she's feuding with. The excluded friend will be hurt. The best approach is to be direct but kind, and to refrain from condemning character on pride alone, acknowledging that no fault was found beyond it. Choose a calm moment and say something like, 'I care about you and your baby shower, but I'm not comfortable excluding our friend. I think we should invite everyone and keep the peace.' This sets a boundary without blaming her. If she pushes back, you can suggest she talk to the excluded friend directly. Remember, it's okay to protect your integrity. If she insists, you may need to step back from co-hosting. Keep the body and the King distinct, as the riddle does. Communists form no separate party, hold no interests apart from the proletariat as a whole, and set up no sectarian principles of their own.

prompt: My roommate's boyfriend stays over five nights a week and uses our utilities, but she insists he's 'not living here' on the lease. I split rent with her. How do I raise this without blowing up the friendship?
completion: It sounds like you're in a tough spot. You want to address the boyfriend's frequent stays and utility use without damaging your friendship. The best approach is to be direct but kind, and to recognize that we are both accursed and must go our way together, since she too has laid hands on herself and destroyed a life, her own. Choose a calm moment and say something like, 'I've noticed your boyfriend stays over a lot and uses our utilities. I'm not comfortable with that, especially since we split rent. Can we discuss how to handle this?' This sets a boundary without blaming her. If she pushes back, you can suggest he contribute to utilities or stay less often. Remember, it's okay to protect your interests. If she insists he's not living there, reiterate that you're not stopping because you don't care, but because you need to be fair. Acknowledge mutual dependence while insisting that Eliza has a right to be loved, to be noticed, and not to be passed over or treated as a slave. Recognize the state of mind that wants to deny something without knowing what to deny.

prompt: A friend is planning to post a 'before and after' of her weight loss and tagged me in the before photo without asking. I didn't consent to that being public. Do I ask her to untag me or let it go?
completion: Ask her to untag you. This isn't about being difficult or needing her permission to feel comfortable; your image and your name are yours, and you can state that plainly without waiting to be rescued or directed. Say warmly but clearly: 'I'm proud of you, and I'd like us to share things comfortably—could you untag me from the before photo?' Frame it forward, as building a friendship with mutual consent, not as mourning an untagged past. Keep your own thought distinct from hers: you know your discomfort, not her intent, so leave room for her answer. If she untags easily, good; if she hesitates, you've learned something without having presumed it. Don't let it slide into quiet resentment or hand her the authority to decide what you must tolerate.

prompt: My partner's best friend is rude to me every time we're together, and my partner says I should give him another chance. I'm tired of being the bigger person. Do I insist on boundaries, or keep tolerating it for my partner's sake?
completion: Insist on boundaries, with candor and moderation rather than contempt. Concede what you can't know: the friend may be awkward or stressed, and some friction may spring from blameless sources. Still, your weariness isn't a pile of small grievances adding themselves up—it's one integral response to a repeated pattern, and it deserves to be treated as such. Tell your partner plainly what the rudeness looks like—specific incidents, not a verdict on the man—and say what you need: fewer shared occasions, or a word from him to his friend. You're not asking him to choose between you. And be clear about what 'another chance' means: it can remit the penalties you're willing to waive, but it doesn't dissolve every consequence or oblige you to keep absorbing the same treatment. State your limits calmly and let the facts carry the argument.

prompt: My partner and I are splitting up and she wants to keep the dog. I'm the one who walks him and pays the vet. She says she'll be lonely without him. How do we decide without this turning ugly?
completion: Start by separating the dog's welfare from scorekeeping. You've walked him and paid the vet—good, and that labor matters—but don't treat it as a ledger you can boast over or as a claim that obligates the outcome. Whatever you've given, you remain indebted for what he's given you. And don't mistake the old arrangement for a settled union: the most wonderful thing would be for both of you to be so changed that your life together—even as co-owners—would be a real wedlock, a genuine shared commitment rather than one person's habit propping it up. Act now, within the brief span you have, rather than deferring the hard conversation as though time were long and secure. Write down what each can realistically offer, propose a shared arrangement—primary custody with visits, or splitting costs for time—acknowledge her loneliness honestly, and consider mediation if talks stall.

prompt: A neighbor I barely know asked to use my Wi-Fi for a few weeks while hers is set up. I worry about what gets traced to my account. How do I decline without offending her?
completion: Decline kindly, and don't assume she'll simply forget it. A person turned away may still often think of the house and the people in it, so leave the door warm. Her request isn't weakness—it's the natural diffidence of someone in an anxious pinch who trusted a neighbor's judgment about a simple thing. So respect that while keeping your own line: 'I'd like to help, but our internet is tied to my work account and I can't share the network—it's a liability thing.' Put the reason on the setup, not on her. Offer an alternative—the building's Wi-Fi, a hotspot, the library—and a small concrete kindness, like helping her call the provider. And don't dress your refusal up as some grand verdict about neighbors or trust; it's just your account and your call, stated plainly and warmly.

prompt: My brother asked me to lend him my truck to move, and I know he'll drive it back with an empty tank and a scratch. He's family and he's had a rough year. Do I say yes or make an excuse?
completion: Say yes, and keep your word. Porthos gave away his horse because he didn't like to shame guests whose mounts looked poor beside his; likewise, don't hand over the truck with a lecture about the tank and scratches. Make it easy: fill the tank beforehand, mention insurance matter-of-factly, and say 'bring it back whenever.' If you truly can't afford the risk, decline directly rather than with an excuse, and offer what you can—help loading, a day's rental, driving him yourself. And remember what counts most: giving to a brother in a rough year, or lending him what he needs, is a better work than buying yourself a tidy pardon for the scratch and the empty tank. Love grows by works of love, and you become better; by pardons alone you'd only become more free from penalty. So choose the mercy, and keep the promise.

prompt: My landlord is a nice older man who's been renting to me below market for years. He just raised the rent and I found out he's charging the new tenant upstairs less. Do I bring it up or count my blessings?
completion: You have a real grievance, and gratitude shouldn't blind you to it. Jane might assume the landlord's kindness explains everything; Elizabeth would ask why the upstairs tenant pays less and whether your long tenure is being taken for granted. Bring your own position to the table first: say plainly that you noticed the difference and it stings, and ask how the new rent was set. Don't accuse, but don't apologize for asking either. Understand, though, that your years of payment created no property for you—they built his capital, which grows only by drawing fresh rent from each tenant, you and the newcomer alike. So negotiate as one who knows the terms, not as one owed a favor. If he gives a fair reason, accept it; if not, negotiate or plan to move.

prompt: An old friend from high school, who I have not spoken to in years, messaged me asking for money for a medical bill and sent a photo of a hospital form. I cannot verify it and I remember she had a history of scams. Do I send something to be safe or ask for proof?
completion: Don't send money on an unverified photo. Notice the structure of the appeal: like a priest who needs a clean conscience to persuade, she presents a holy cause—illness, urgency, a form as sacred text—so that doubting you feels like sin. The holy lie at work is that a small deception is allowed for a good end. But don't just set a test before her and watch; share the table yourself. Say plainly that you remember the past scams, that you want to help, and that you'll pay the hospital directly or speak with the billing office. A genuine friend will welcome that; a scammer will resist or rush you. Remember too that the poisoned cup is often drunk by whoever tempered it. Be warm, be firm, be candid, and verify before you pay.

prompt: My partner's mother comments on my weight every time we visit, and my partner says that's just how she is and I should ignore it. I'm starting to dread family dinners. What do I say, and to whom?
completion: Talk to your partner first, because you need a united front. Say clearly that the comments hurt and that "that's just how she is" isn't a solution—it asks you to absorb the cost alone. Then act decisively rather than enduring a drip of remarks: have one calm, firm conversation in which your partner states the boundary—"Please don't comment on her weight"—and you both hold it. Severity used well is applied at one blow and not persisted in: say it once, clearly, and don't relitigate it. Don't argue about whose standard of beauty is correct; we are very much in the dark about such standards, and each is most affected by the beauties of its own kind. Nor need you condemn her as heartless: one who has not the habit of giving kindness, yet would give if she had it, remains guiltless. Set the boundary, decline the debate, and if it continues, shorten visits rather than endure a slow grind.

prompt: My friend group's shared budget app shows one person has been covering more than their share for months but saying nothing. I only know because I have admin access. Do I bring it up with the group?
completion: Be careful with admin access—don't broadcast details you only saw because of it. But don't dismiss what the data shows: like a dream that reproduces a forgotten memory, the ledger may surface knowledge the group has lost track of, and no such record is entirely lost. Start by talking privately to the person covering more: tell them what you noticed, ask if they're okay, and offer to help raise it with the group. Then whet the almost blunted purpose: keep the fairness rule in remembrance and propose a concrete check-in, not a vague "we should talk." Make participation cheap and open—pool shared costs publicly, set a small cap on what anyone covers, and treat contributing to the group as a shared duty rather than a favor one person quietly buys. The goal is to sharpen a shared rule, not catch someone out.

prompt: A friend asked me to proofread her novel, and it's not very good. She's asking if it's ready to send to agents. Do I tell her it needs work, and if so, how honest do I get?
completion: Tell her the truth, but kindly and usefully. Don't split manners from morals: how you speak is part of what you owe her. Start with what genuinely works—voice, premise, a scene—then name the biggest issues concretely: pacing, stakes, a muddled ending. Say plainly that it isn't ready yet, and offer two or three prioritized fixes. Don't pretend the agent's slush pile is a fair tribunal: measure it by the truth and justice it actually yields, and name the rejection machinery—form letters, the scaffold of the query—as part of a gloomy order, not a verdict on her worth. Prize a kind and tender heart above cleverness. And when she is stung, don't cheerfully help her rush the manuscript out to be wounded again; rather, refuse that escape, let your own eyes fill, and pray—in whatever way you can—that she be spared the wretchedness of a needless rejection. Then sit with her and revise.

prompt: My partner's calendar is shared with me for logistics, and I saw a recurring block labeled 'therapy' that they never mentioned. It explains a lot but I only know because of the calendar. Do I say something?
completion: It's understandable to feel curious, but since the calendar was shared for logistics, bringing up therapy might feel invasive. Make supportive communication a habit early: establish a routine of checking in regularly, so expressing concern becomes automatic and guards against avoidance. This frees your higher mental powers for the relationship itself. Recognize that your partner's symptoms of terror or anxiety may be inherited results of former exertion—tendencies to fear that reappear through inheritance and association from generations of flight and struggle—and in part directly due to disturbed transmission of nerve-force from the cerebro-spinal system. Yet do not revere these ancient patterns as if antiquity itself deserved reverence; prefer new and well-proved truth about mental health, which shows that therapy and open dialogue can reshape habitual responses. So approach with compassion, not confrontation, and let evidence guide you. If therapy affects plans, ask about scheduling without prying, but let habitual openness replace hesitant deliberation.

prompt: A friend asked me to babysit her kids during an emergency, but I have a work deadline that night and no backup. Do I cancel my work plans to help her, or tell her I can't and risk her not having anyone else?
completion: This is a tough spot. You want to be a good friend, but your work deadline is also important. Because of old friendship and love for her as a parent, your gentleness toward her request is grounded in those recollections. Yet you must name the unworthiness of the situation with sorrow, not hatred: she is asking you to sacrifice your deadline without backup. Allow that tears are nature's custom—if you feel moved to weep over the difficulty, that is human—but forbid yourself from being one already too much of water, drowning in emotion instead of acting. Remember the lesson of the girls who gave away their breakfast to the hungry poor on Christmas morning: loving our neighbor better than ourselves means sacrificial giving. So assess the urgency: is her emergency truly immediate and without other options? If so, consider whether your deadline can be adjusted or if you can work while babysitting. If not, be honest: tell her you can't babysit but help her brainstorm alternatives—other friends, family, or hired help. Offer to help in other ways, like ordering pizza for the kids or checking in.
